blocks.title: Industry & analogy
blocks.subtitle: Who is moving on the grid, who is stacking capacity — and why the forms still miss the peril.

blocks.text: The connections clearing fastest are non-firm — interruptible by contract. The market prices damage; the peril is availability.
The collision

Britain is connecting tens of gigawatts of data-centre and energy load to a grid that can no longer promise to keep it switched on. Compute is a 24/7, always-on consumer that monetises every hour — so for the first time the demand side is paying a premium for firmness itself, and the data-centre build-out has put that load at the front of a queue the network cannot firmly serve.{{cite:INDUSTRY-DC-COMPUTE-DEMAND,ACAD-CCM-NF-LOAD}} Non-firm risk is not an old peril rediscovered; it is a new one, created by the collision of an always-on demand curve with an interruptible grid.
One template, three industries
When always-on load met an interruptible grid

The London energy market grew up on a damage template that still dominates today. Power and renewables were underwritten on all-risks physical damage, machinery breakdown and delay-in-start-up wordings built for turbines, transformers and construction phases — perils with a proximate cause an adjuster can find.{{cite:LMA-BI-GUIDE,EPIC-DC-ENERGY-RISK}} When a wind farm was curtailed, the revenue shortfall sat in merchant power economics or a PPA, not in a time-element clause: the form never expected lawful switch-off as the loss mechanism. Flexible connections did not rewrite the binder; they simply fed more assets through the same damage-first stack.

Data centres inherited that stack and scaled it. Property all-risks and business interruption still anchor the tower; broker facilities now quote multi-billion-dollar lifecycle capacity for hyperscale campuses while carrier research sizes a premium pool toward tens of billions as AI load concentrates insurable values.{{cite:BROK-MARSH-NIMBUS,AON-DCLP,SP-HYPERSCALE-INSURABLE-POOL,SWISS-RE-DATA-CENTRE-AI}} The sophisticated placement already negotiates utility-failure NDBI, contingent business interruption on energy providers, and parametric SLA mirrors tied to uptime telemetry — but the grid-curtailment index the connection agreement encodes rarely appears in the schedule.{{cite:BROK-LOCKTON-SLA,MGA-PARAMETRIX-SLA,INSTECH-NDBI-PARAMETRIC}} Power is already the largest driver of significant data-centre outages;{{cite:ACAD-DC-OUTAGE}} the market prices the building and the cable fault, not the operator's lawful instruction to switch off.

That history is the mispricing. Each sector received capacity on instruments built for breaking things, while the fastest-growing loss is availability without damage. Curtailment cost is observable in the system operator's constraint accounts;{{cite:NESO-CONSTRAINT-COSTS}} SLA breach math is contractual;{{cite:ACAD-EXPONENTIAL-PARETO-SLA-PREMIUM}} yet the premium function on most energy and property schedules still evaluates physical cause alone. The gap is not under-rating a known peril — it is writing zero premium on a peril the form cannot trigger.
Three industries, one damage template — and a new loss that none of them were built to see.
Grid runs ahead of wording
Reform on the wire, silence in the wording

The grid side is not waiting. A 2025 synthesis of global non-firm access identifies four dominant models — capacity-limited, time-limited, dynamic operating envelopes, and fully flexible active network management — now written into law or code from Great Britain through Spain, Germany, Belgium, and Australia.{{cite:ACAD-NONFIRM-REVIEW,OFGEM-ACCESS-SCR}} Britain's Flexible Plug and Play pilots cut connection cost by up to 87% and lead times by 57% by accepting curtailable access instead of reinforcement; Ofgem's Access SCR then standardised that trade for larger users, with curtailment limits and end-dates in the connection offer the loss adjuster can read but the BI wording cannot trigger on.{{cite:ACAD-NONFIRM-REVIEW,OFGEM-ACCESS-SCR}} The EU's 2024 electricity-market directive now requires Member States to offer flexible connections where capacity is scarce — interruptibility is becoming a register fact, not a negotiated footnote.{{cite:EU-DIRECTIVE-FLEX-ACCESS,ACAD-NONFIRM-REVIEW}}

The insurance side is moving on a parallel track, but toward capacity not trigger fit. In roughly eighteen months the London and Bermuda markets have stacked specialist facilities — Marsh's $2.7bn Nimbus programme, Aon's $3.5bn data-centre lifecycle facility, parametric SLA mirrors from Lloyd's coverholders — while S&P Global sizes a ~$10bn premium runway for hyperscale campuses and Swiss Re warns of a ~$10bn single nat-cat tail on a US data centre.{{cite:BROK-MARSH-NIMBUS,AON-DCLP,SP-HYPERSCALE-INSURABLE-POOL,SWISS-RE-DATA-CENTRE-AI,MGA-PARAMETRIX-SLA}} Almost all of it still routes through all-risks physical-damage and time-element wordings; the curtailment-predictability spectrum the grid regulators now encode has no mirror in the binder.{{cite:LMA-BI-GUIDE,ACAD-NONFIRM-REVIEW}}

Insurance has climbed this ladder before, but never on availability. Generation 1.0 is the damage-linked business-interruption stack — physical cause, adjuster proof, decades of loss history.{{cite:LMA-BI-GUIDE}} 1.5 adds contingent and non-damage BI extensions — utility failure, energy-provider CBI — but still waits on proximate breakage or an insured peril. 2.0 is parametric SLA and index mirrors: telemetry pays without an adjuster, but the index is usually uptime at the rack, not curtailment at the boundary.{{cite:MGA-PARAMETRIX-SLA,BROK-LOCKTON-SLA,DESCARTES-DC-PARAMETRIC}} 3.0 — the generation the grid is forcing — ties the trigger to register-native firmness: gate status, curtailment cap, boundary congestion. The market is still selling 1.0 into a 3.0 peril.
Why London hasn't priced it
Why London still prices damage, not availability

There is no shortage of energy-insurance capacity in London. Dozens of carriers, Lloyd's syndicates, MGAs and brokers write power, renewables and construction risk every day. So why does an unpriced peril survive inside a sophisticated market? Three structural reasons, none of them stupidity. First, the form is sticky: energy cover is sold on all-risks physical-damage-and-time-element wordings refined over decades, and a curtailment generates no damage event for a loss adjuster to find.{{cite:LMA-BI-GUIDE}} Second, the incentives point sideways: an underwriter is rewarded for growing premium on a familiar form, not for inventing an availability product whose loss history does not yet exist. Third, the peril is new: the always-on compute load that makes firmness valuable is a phenomenon of the last few years, and rates lag exposure by exactly the interval it takes a loss to show up in the triangles.

The specialist market is racing to add limit, not fit: broker facilities quote billions in aggregate data-centre capacity, carrier research sizes double-digit premium runways, and parametric SLA products exist in fragments — but the connection agreement's curtailment cap, end-date, and predictability class rarely appear in the schedule.{{cite:BROK-MARSH-NIMBUS,AON-DCLP,SP-HYPERSCALE-INSURABLE-POOL,MGA-PARAMETRIX-SLA}} Curtailment cost is already observable in the system operator's constraint-cost data{{cite:NESO-CONSTRAINT-COSTS}} — yet almost none of it flows into an energy premium. That gap between an observable, rising cost and a flat rate is the definition of mispricing.

The trade is not a macro bet on energy but a placement question: where to deploy rated capacity next. If damage-BI underprices curtailment — which rising constraint costs and flat BI rates suggest — then carriers and MGAs already in generation 2.0 (parametric SLA, index mirrors) earn the roll-up; composite writers stacking DC limits on 1.0 wordings carry silent accumulation.{{cite:NESO-CONSTRAINT-COSTS,SP-HYPERSCALE-INSURABLE-POOL,MGA-PARAMETRIX-SLA}} Whitespace on this index is not absence of risk: it is preparedness without a matching exposure, or exposure the market has not yet repriced. Which leg moves first when Gate 2 status lands on renewal determines who looks cheap and who looks caught.
Same peril, four layers of the chain — each carrying it in a different form.

blocks.title: The landscape
blocks.subtitle: Map the field before you score it — who sits where in the value chain, and how the population spreads on two axes.

blocks.text: Four layers, one peril
Four layers, one peril

The same peril sits differently at each link of the chain, and preparedness at one layer does not imply it at the next. A carrier can be capital-strong while the MGA binding its energy facility has no availability wording; a colocation asset can be heavily exposed while the reinsurer behind the cedant models only physical cat.

The London market publishes hazard scores, rating-agency capital, and broker line-cards — but no comparable field map of non-firm exposure versus preparedness across carriers, MGAs, brokers, assets and reinsurers on the same axes. Cat vendors sell modules; brokers sell facilities; parametric MGAs sell index products. None of them plot the whole population on availability risk with register-backed sub-factors and explicit evidence tiers. That map is what this index is: not a replacement for underwriting judgement, but the only plane on which to compare posture before the peril has a loss triangle.

blocks.caption: Each layer carries non-firm power risk in a different form — scored on its own Exposure and Preparedness.

items.name: Carriers & Lloyd's syndicates
items.role: Hold the balance sheet. Exposure is the concentration of energy / data-centre / specialty premium in the book; preparedness is capital strength, availability products, and the expertise to price curtailment rather than damage.
items.examples: Composite insurers, London-market specialty carriers, Lloyd's syndicates

items.name: MGAs & brokers
items.role: Price and place without (mostly) carrying the balance sheet. Exposure is the risk routed through their facilities and binders; preparedness is the products they can actually structure and the talent to broke an availability tower.
items.examples: Delegated-authority MGAs, wholesale and London-chain brokers

items.name: Energy & data-centre assets
items.role: Originate the peril. Exposure is the share of capacity on flexible / non-firm connections and queue position; preparedness is backup generation, monitoring, and how firmly the connection is secured.
items.examples: Hyperscale & colocation campuses, batteries, generation behind a non-firm connection

items.name: Reinsurers & capacity
items.role: Stand behind the carriers. Exposure is correlated tail risk aggregated across cedants on the same constrained network; preparedness is rated capital and the modelling to see the correlation the primary market misses.
items.examples: Property-cat and specialty reinsurers, retrocession capacity

blocks.text: The Non-Firm Power Insurance Risk Index scores this population from the outside in — {{fact:total}} entities on two axes the market does not yet publish together, read as a margin rather than a hazard rank. The sections that follow set the frame and prosecute the case; the scatter plots every scored name on that plane — each dot a posture on exposure and preparedness, not a pecking order.

In competitive terms the scatter is a placement map, not a league table. Whitespace syndicates sit beside parametric MGAs that already close the trigger gap but lack balance-sheet scale; exposed composite writers stack billion-dollar DC limits beside carriers whose linked L3 assets show deeper negative margins than the headline score. A broker structuring an availability tower needs both views — who can sign the paper, and whether the assets behind them share a constraint boundary.
Map the chain first; then read exposure against preparedness for every name in the universe.
